name: Sortino ratio
definition: Sortino is arithmetic mean return above a fixed target divided by downside deviation below that target, with an explicitly stated period and denominator convention.
explanation: The target defines a shortfall. In this worksheet, returns at or above it contribute zero and all observations remain in the downside denominator. The arithmetic mean-minus-target numerator can be negative. Zero downside deviation leaves the quotient undefined. Standard deviation around the mean is a different risk measure, and the period result is not automatically annualized.
formula: Period Sortino = (mean return − target) / sqrt(Σ min(return − target, 0)² / N).
formulaNote: Here N includes every observation; return, target and deviation use matching periods and percentage-point units.

pitfall.title: A positive return can still fall below the target
pitfall.text: A 0.5% monthly return is a shortfall against a 1% monthly target. Counting only negative returns, or dividing only by the count of losing observations, changes the measure.

name: Gross rent multiplier (GRM)
definition: Gross rent multiplier is a property price divided by annual gross rent. This worksheet uses scheduled whole-property rent before vacancy and expense deductions.
explanation: The annual denominator makes monthly and annual rent quotes comparable after converting units. Its reciprocal times 100 gives gross annual rent yield, not cap rate or net rental yield. Reverse calculations express a chosen multiplier as an implied price or required rent. Comparable-property evidence, expense analysis and market judgment remain separate.
formula: GRM = property price / annual gross scheduled rent; gross annual rent yield (%) = 100 / GRM.
formulaNote: Multiply monthly gross rent by 12 first. Gross scheduled rent is not net operating income, and the multiplier is not a payback period.

pitfall.title: The multiplier does not reveal net return
pitfall.text: A GRM of 12.5 compares price with one year of gross rent. It does not deduct vacancy, operating costs, capital work, financing or tax and cannot establish a 12.5-year payback.

name: Debt-to-equity ratio
definition: Debt-to-equity compares a clearly defined company liability or borrowing amount with matching shareholders’ equity. This worksheet uses book equity and identifies total-liabilities and interest-bearing-debt numerators separately.
explanation: The ratio is sensitive to both definitions and balance-sheet events. Repaying a liability from existing cash reduces cash and that liability without creating equity in this model. A new equity injection retained as cash increases equity. Zero or negative book equity needs explicit investigation rather than a favorable negative leverage score.
formula: D/E = selected total liabilities or interest-bearing debt / positive book shareholders’ equity.
formulaNote: Use one reporting date, currency and company scope. Borrowing / (borrowing + equity) can exclude other liabilities and is not automatically borrowing / total assets.

pitfall.title: A different debt definition can explain a different ratio
pitfall.text: $240,000 total liabilities and $160,000 equity give 1.5. If only $160,000 interest-bearing debt is selected for the same equity, the ratio is 1.0. The company did not change; the numerator did.
